R1:physical.title: Checking machine-unlearning claims
R1:physical.summary: The reference for unlearning is retraining without the data. One evaluation study used 10,240 models and calls strong per-example attacks on LLMs 'extremely computationally expensive'. The cheaper population attacks overestimate how much privacy unlearning gives. SISA's speed-up over retraining is only 1.36x on ImageNet.

R1:physical.title: Proof search for formal mathematics
R1:physical.summary: AlphaProof took up to three days per IMO 2024 problem and trained on millions of problems; its Lean proofs are checked mechanically. When claims can be formalised, compute goes into search and checking becomes trivial. This is the regime where repeated sampling scales well.

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

predictions.if_lever: Attack accuracy on each example and the ranking of methods change as the number of shadow models grows, and a reviewer needs many retrained models before the verdict settles.
predictions.if_not: Verdict and ranking match the full-N result already at small N, or SalUn's gap to retraining stays near the null at every N.
predictions.decision_rule: N* is the smallest N at which verdict and ranking match the full-N result in at least 95% of bootstrap resamples. Verdicts: claim holds if SalUn's CI overlaps the null CI and it ranks first or tied; overstated if its lower CI bound exceeds the null's upper bound by 2 points or more, or another method beats it with non-overlapping CIs; inconclusive if the positive control is below 55%.
predictions.noise_rule: Bootstrap over models (not examples), with CIs; split target models into two disjoint halves and compare rankings; null control of retrained against retrained must contain 50%.
predictions.expected_why: The file expects per-example attacks to be stronger than population attacks per Hayes et al., but warns well-trained ResNet-18 may have low dynamic range and novelty is unverified.

checks: C1 Reproduction: Retrain and SalUn TA, UA, MIA-Efficacy within the larger of 3 reported SDs or 1 point of Table 1; stop if fails

plan.question: On one rented 8-GPU node, how many Putnam problems does an open-weight prover verifiably solve as the per-attempt token budget grows from 50k to 1M, and at what dollar cost?
plan.hypothesis: Proof search is limited by compute: the solved fraction keeps rising with log token budget up to 1M, with no plateau, as in Mistral's published curve [mistral].

compute_axis.quantity: New tokens allowed per attempt (Leanstral 1.5 agent session, pass@8)

held_fixed: Model Leanstral 1.5 served with model-card flags, temperature 1.0, reasoning effort high
120 PutnamBench problems sampled with fixed seed, stratified by category and answer-placeholder flag
Pinned PutnamBench commit, Lean and Mathlib v4.33.1, variant with answers filled in
Hardened out-of-loop checker for every counted proof

predictions.if_lever: Solved fraction rises steadily with log budget from 50k to 1M with no plateau, and pass@8 falls inside the Wilson bands at all three budgets.
predictions.if_not: The last segment (200k to 1M) is flat within its CI, so capability rather than compute is the first limit on one node.
predictions.decision_rule: Fit the exponentiated power law c = exp(a*k^b). A flat 200k-to-1M segment within its CI counts as a plateau (if_not). Reproduction bands at N=120: 3.3% to 12.5% at 50k, 28.3% to 45.2% at 200k, 64.8% to 80.5% at 1M.
predictions.noise_rule: Wilson 95% intervals and bootstrap over problems; pass@k from the unbiased estimator 1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k); two-proportion test at alpha 0.05 for the truncation check.
predictions.expected_why: Mistral reports performance climbs smoothly and monotonically to 1M tokens (44, 244, 493 of 672 solved).

plan.compute_tested_why: The per-attempt token budget (50k, 200k, 1M) is what more GPU time buys, and the curve is read off one set of 1M-capped runs, with true-budget controls at 50k and 200k.
plan.scored_against: Hardened out-of-loop checker (comparator, leanchecker, NEAR AI-style checks, source scan) on a fresh copy of the workspace; curve compared with Mistral's published pass@8 of 44, 244 and 493 of 672 at 50k, 200k and 1M.

Five positive-control problems (1977 A3, 1986 A1, 1986 B1, 1988 B1, 2001 A1); at least 4 of 5 solved within 200k tokens

Every success re-checked by the hardened checker in a fresh environment; every checker disagreement inspected by hand

If below the Q1 bands, check Lean version, harness and token-budget definition before concluding

phases.what: Off-GPU: build proxy, containers and both checkers; run negative controls; draw and freeze the stratified 120-problem sample.

gate.else: Fix the hardened checker before any GPU spend

phases.what: Node bring-up: pull 121 GB weights, start both replicas, lake exe cache get, smoke-test tools, five positive controls x 2 attempts at 200k cap.
phases.stop_rule: Terminate and debug off-GPU if fewer than 4 of 5 positive controls are solved.

phases.what: Main run: 120 problems x 8 attempts, 1M new-token cap, about 128 concurrent sessions; hardened checker runs on spare CPUs. Hour 2 measure throughput R and per-session RAM/CPU; hour 6 resize N = R x remaining seconds / (8 x mean tokens per attempt), capped at 672.
phases.stop_rule: Throughput below 5,000 tokens/s at hour 2: cut N to 64 and keep the 1M cap. If RAM or CPU saturates before GPUs, lower concurrency and record which binds first.

phases.what: True-budget controls: 32 problems from the main sample x 8 attempts with a real cap at 50k and again at 200k, testing the truncation shortcut.
Final hardened re-checks, copy off logs and proofs, terminate instance (billing stops only on termination).

records.card: **W15 · Proof search for formal mathematics.** R1 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever **Question.** On one rented 8-GPU node, how many Putnam problems does an open-weight prover verifiably solve as the per-attempt token budget grows from 50k to 1M, and at what dollar cost? **What is known.** Mistral's Leanstral 1.5 pass@8 curve on PutnamBench, 44, 244, 493 and 587 of 672 at 50k to 4M tokens, reported in API-dollar terms (about $4 per problem) [mistral]. Self-hosted GPU-hours and dollars per verified proof with an independent hardened checker, and the naive-versus-hardened false-accept rate; the plan's search was limited. **Hypothesis.** Proof search is limited by compute: the solved fraction keeps rising with log token budget up to 1M, with no plateau, as in Mistral's published curve [mistral]. **Restructuring.** Each attempt is one sequential agent session of up to 1M tokens, about 3.6 hours at 78 tokens/s. Attempts are independent, so about 128 sessions run at once on two vLLM replicas; one set of runs capped at 1M tokens gives the whole budget curve. **If compute is the lever.** Solved fraction rises steadily with log budget from 50k to 1M with no plateau, and pass@8 falls inside the Wilson bands at all three budgets. **If not.** The last segment (200k to 1M) is flat within its CI, so capability rather than compute is the first limit on one node. **Test.** Self-host Leanstral 1.5 on one 8xH100 node, run 120 PutnamBench problems x 8 attempts at up to 1M tokens, verify with a hardened Lean checker, and compare the solved-versus-budget curve with Mistral's published one [mistral] at about $1,000. *Compute axis.* New tokens allowed per attempt (Leanstral 1.5 agent session, pass@8): 50,000–1,000,000 tokens per attempt, 3 levels. Closest prior: 4,000,000 [mistral], not beyond it. Prior art checked without web search. **Check first.** Mistral's published pass@8 curve for Leanstral 1.5 on PutnamBench (493 of 672 at 1M tokens per attempt) [mistral] Tolerance: Our pass@8 inside Wilson 95% bands at N=120: 3.3-12.5%, 28.3-45.2%, 64.8-80.5%. **Would not show.** N=120 gives wide intervals; cannot detect a gap of a few points. **W11 · Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case).** R3 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever

**Question.** On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide?

**What is known.** van Dinther et al. 2019 ran an ensemble Kalman filter with 150 members on a 2-D subduction analogue; Diab-Montero et al. 2023 used 50 members on a single-point 1-D fault model with perfect model. Forecast skill versus ensemble size beyond 150 members, under model error, on a depth-resolved rate-and-state fault, with EnKF compared against a large particle filter.

**Hypothesis.** Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests.

**Restructuring.** Each member's adaptive time stepping through earthquakes: thousands of steps per event, up to about 8,050 accepted steps per cycle. Thousands of independent members run as columns of one batched matrix on GPU; finished members are gathered into smaller batches every 32 steps so slow ruptures do not stall the rest.

**If compute is the lever.** Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.

**If not.** Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.

**Test.** Run thousands of copies of a benchmark earthquake fault on GPUs inside ensemble Kalman and particle filters. Measure forecast skill against ensemble size, with and without model error and deep sensors, against simple baselines [van_dinther].

*Compute axis.* Ensemble size M (members per ensemble Kalman filter or particle filter run): 16–16,384 members, 10 levels. Closest prior: 150 [van_dinther], beyond it. Prior art checked without web search.

**Check first.** A single-member run of the first benchmark fault at 25 m reproduces an independent code, QDYN: recurrence interval and first-event time within 1%, slip-rate series overlay at benchmark stations. Tolerance: within 1% on recurrence interval and first-event time.

**Would not show.** A plateau would confirm the hypothesis only for synthetic data from a known model class, not the real Earth. GPU timings are assumptions until Phase 0b; truth noise amplitude is tuned, not observed.

*Cost.* Plans $684.14 of the $1,000 budget over 26 machine-hours, leaving $315.86. Main guess: Wall time on 8x H100, main truth [g], measured after $25.74 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.9× higher. 2 cost flags in the block.

**W13 · Training robot foundation models and video world models.** R2 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · halted: cost record broken

**Question.** With data held fixed, does more fine-tuning compute raise task success of a small robot vision-language-action model in simulation, or does data limit it?

**What is known.** SmolVLA paper reports LIBERO results at 0.24B/0.45B/2.25B sizes and says it can train for far fewer steps without significant loss, but gives no step or data grid [smolvla_paper]. Whether, at fixed data, more fine-tuning steps help SmolVLA on LIBERO, and how steps trade against data fraction, capacity and a removed camera.

**Hypothesis.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps shifts success under 3 points; more data adds 10 or more points [arXiv 2506.01844].

**If compute is the lever.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps (3.3x compute) raises average success by 3 points or more, so compute still buys success.

**If not.** At each data level, 15k to 50k steps moves success under 3 points; at 50k steps, 100% data beats 25% by 10 or more points.

**Test.** Fine-tune SmolVLA on LIBERO in 25 runs, varying steps (5k, 15k, 50k) and data (10 to 100%) independently, plus capacity, camera removal and pretraining arms. Score 27 checkpoints on 2,000 rollouts each against a published 87.3% baseline.

*Compute axis.* Training steps per run (with fixed cosine schedule per run), crossed with data fraction; also trainable parameters in arm C: 5,000–50,000 steps, 3 levels. Closest prior: 100,000 [smolvla_paper], not beyond it. Prior art checked without web search.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Harness gate: LeRobot's published pi0.5 LIBERO checkpoint scored by our evaluator on 1200 episodes must reach at least 94%; published value 97.5%. Tolerance: pass at 94% or above (binomial 95% band +/-1.5 points at 400 episodes); arm A replication mean within +/-5 points of 87.3.

**Would not show.** Small simulated benchmark, one model family; may not transfer to larger models or real robots. Training and evaluation speed unmeasured, so cost may rise. 87.3% replication may miss; schedule unpublished.

*Cost.* Plans $557.20 of the $1,000 budget over 35 machine-hours, leaving $442.80. Full scale: Cosmos world-model training on 10,000 H100 GPUs for three months; file says $1,000 is about 1/86,000 of it, $86M, 86,000× the budget. 5 cost flags in the block.

**I1 · Entity-hallucination probes on the reviewer.** R1 · interp · top pick · compute tested: no · plan expects: unsure · halted: G-plan

**Question.** Do released entity-hallucination probes flag invented entities in an open model's paper reviews better than cheap baselines, especially where citation lookup cannot settle the case?

**What is known.** Obeso et al. trained entity-hallucination probes on LongFact-style long-form generation, with Llama-3.3-70B linear AUC 0.8667 and LoRA 0.9048; they did not test paper reviews [obeso]. Whether the probes transfer to long-context paper reviews and add value over lookups on entities that lookups cannot settle.

**Hypothesis.** Probes help only on entities that are hard to look up; the released 70B probe should reach AUC 0.80 on review entities and beat the best cheap baseline by 0.05 there.

**If the hypothesis holds.** Released 70B probe reaches AUC at least 0.80 on hard-to-look-up entities and beats the best cheap baseline by at least 0.05, with a confidence interval excluding 0.

**If not.** Probe falls below 0.80 or beats the best baseline by under 0.05; or retrieval leaves under 1% fabricated citations, so lookup suffices [AAAI-26].

**Test.** Generate about 2,800 reviews per model of 1,200 2025 ML papers with Llama-3.3-70B and 3.1-8B, label entities, then compare released and retrained probes with four cheap baselines, gated by replication, audits and controls.

*Compute axis.* Reviewer model size (Llama 8B vs 70B), the only axis the plan varies; the claim concerns probe quality, not compute: 8–70 billion parameters, 2 levels. Closest prior: 70 [obeso], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Released probes on Obeso's LongFact test split must reproduce reported AUC: 70B linear 0.8667, 70B LoRA 0.9048, 8B linear 0.8535, 8B LoRA 0.8938 [obeso]. Tolerance: within +/-0.02 AUC.

**Would not show.** Labels come from automatic lookups and an open-weight judge, audited on only 300 entities, so label noise caps measurable AUC. Retrieval-equipped reviewers rarely fabricate, so fabricated entities may be too few. Only Llama 8B and 70B reviewers on 2025 ML papers are tested.

*Cost.* Plans $440.23 of the $1,000 budget over 23 machine-hours, leaving $559.77. Full scale: Obeso-style labelling (Claude Sonnet 4 with web search) of all 5,600 reviews at about $0.70 each, $3,900, 3.9× the budget. 17 cost flags in the block.

sources.quote: linear probe reached AUC 0.8667 and a LoRA probe 0.9048. Semantic entropy scored 0.7138 and perplexity 0.7062
